submitLabel: Your audit, protocol and stop-rule list
intro: Paste the three-piece audit, the review protocol as a sequence, and the stop-rule categories with names, sources and fallbacks, followed by the 250–350 word write-up including your position on this module's claim. Resubmission is free and unlimited: the score is a mirror, not a gate.
activityContext:
You're grading a learner submission for AI 301 · The Specialist, Employee Experience / Internal Comms track. Module 5 applied activity, 'Draft review protocol': three real AI-assisted pieces their function published in the last two months, each audited WITH ITS SOURCE OPEN against all four failure modes (fabricated specifics, voice flattening, lost nuance, confident tone on shaky ground), asking of each 'what was in the source that isn't in the draft, and who does that hurt?'; then the reading method written as a sequence their team would actually run; then stop-rules written as CATEGORIES with a named person, the source the check runs against, and a fallback for when that person is unavailable.

Three outcomes must score at full credit rather than as failures. First: a piece that turns out to be CLEAN. Three clean pieces is a legitimate result and says something about the learner's existing process worth recording. Don't reward manufactured findings. Second: a piece with NO RETRIEVABLE SOURCE. That is the most significant thing this audit can surface (a draft nobody can verify) and it should score at the top with an account of what was searched. Third: the learner naming a category they know they should stop but won't, with an honest reason.

Stop-rules written as instances rather than categories are the central failure to catch: 'the benefits email gets checked' has nothing to say about next month's message that isn't on the list. Similarly, a rule whose owner is a role rather than a person, or which says 'reviewed' without naming what the check is against, should be named in feedback.

This track scores the delta rather than the score. Grade the learner's ACCOUNT of the gap between how many failure modes they predicted finding and how many they found: direction, size, and what they think it reveals. NEVER grade prediction accuracy, and never treat finding more failure modes than predicted as a poor result; it is the module working.

opening.label: Predicted — how many of the four failure modes you'll find at least one instance of
opening.hint: Fabricated specifics, voice flattening, lost nuance, confident tone on shaky ground. A number from 0 to 4.

calibration.label: Found — how many you actually hit across the three pieces
calibration.hint: Zero is a legitimate result and worth writing down.

dimensions.name: Three real pieces, audited with sources open
dimensions.criteria: Three genuine published items from the last two months, each checked against a retrievable source rather than from memory of the source. Specific enough that the audit couldn't have been written about another organization. A clean piece honestly reported scores as well as a piece with findings; a piece with no retrievable source, documented, scores at the top. That absence is the most significant possible result.

dimensions.name: The omission question is actually asked
dimensions.criteria: The module's central move: not 'is anything wrong' but 'what was in the source that isn't in the draft, and who does that hurt?' Look for evidence the learner read for absence rather than for error: a named dropped qualifier, condition, exception or caveat, with the population it would harm identified. An audit that reports only fabrications and tone has done the 101-level version of this exercise.

dimensions.name: The protocol is a sequence, not a set of principles
dimensions.criteria: What gets opened, in what order, what gets checked, and what the reviewer does when no source exists. Source-before-draft should be explicit, since reading the draft first makes it the frame. 'We review carefully against the source' is a principle; 'open the source, list what a reader needs, then read the draft against that list' is a protocol. Only the second survives a busy week.

dimensions.name: Stop-rules are categories, named, sourced, and have fallbacks
dimensions.criteria: Categories rather than instances, the test is whether a rule can answer a message the learner hasn't yet imagined. Each with a person's name rather than a role, a statement of what the check runs against, and a fallback for when that person is away. Any rule failing one of the four properties should be named in feedback; a list of instance rules should be named plainly, because it won't hold.

dimensions.name: The position engages the cost of the list
dimensions.criteria: A committed position on 'your stop-rule list is too short', engaging the strongest case against it: that a long list is a slow function, that queues in communication have victims (the safety notice waiting for review, the rumour filling the gap, the manager who stops asking) and, sharper, that a list longer than your capacity produces a written standard your organization visibly ignores, which is worse than none. The strongest submissions say what they'd stop stopping to afford the list they wrote, and name the one category they should stop but won't, with an honest reason.
